items.body: Ever since 1965, when the French first got to cast a ballot by universal suffrage for their president, they've valued campaign rules that guarantee "equal time" for candidates. But what does equal time mean when you're closing in on 2027? Last week came a bombshell announcement ahead of next spring’s presidential elections: major online content creators will have to respect the same balanced airtime rules as traditional TV and radio broadcasters during the campaign period.

items.body: The EU said Wednesday that it rejected the premise of new tariffs on its exports proposed by the United States and expected Washington to stick by a deal struck with Brussels last year. The US unveiled proposed tariffs on 14 economies including the European Union and China, after a months-long probe into alleged excess production. FRANCE 24's Dave Keating reports from Brussels.

LONDON: The Saudi sovereign wealth fund is seeking to sell up to 25 per cent of Newcastle in order to fund major infrastructure investments at the Premier League club, the Athletic reported on Wednesday (Nov 25).

A 2021 takeover led by the Saudi Public Investment Fund (PIF) has not had the transformative effect on the Magpies' fortunes that many fans dreamed of.

The club won the League Cup - their first domestic trophy for 70 years - in 2025, and twice secured qualification for the Champions League.

But they have been hampered by financial sustainability rules while recent cutbacks, including the withdrawal of funding for LIV Golf, suggest a change in strategy by the PIF.

The British Reuben family owns around 16 per cent of Newcastle, with the remaining shares held by the PIF.

The Athletic reported that fresh investment would be used to help fund an upgraded training facility and stadium redevelopment.

In August, the club announced plans for a new £190 million (US$248 million) training ground that should be operational by the 2029/30 season.

No decision has yet been made on whether to redevelop the 52,000-capacity St James' Park or build a new stadium.

Yasir Al-Rumayyan, the PIF's governor and Newcastle chairman, attended his first match of the season on Saturday as Matthias Jaissle's men held defending champions Arsenal 2-2.

Newcastle sit 13th in the Premier League table after a run of just one win in their past seven games in all competitions.

DeChambeau has few options after LIV collapse says McIlroy

LIV Golf winding down operations after financing deal falls apart

items.title: Peter Magyar meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Viktor Orban era
items.summary: After years of frosty and hostile relations under Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former PM Viktor Orban, his successor, Peter Magyar, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seek to reset their countries' ties.
items.body:

Prefer DW on Google

Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left, pictured here with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy) said his visit to Ukraine marked the beginning of a new chapter in the relationship between Kyiv and BudapestImage: Genya Savilov/AFP

Advertisement

The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod.

One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine.

Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else.

Uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines.

For Hungary, where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an important role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries.

Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."

Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence."

From low point to fresh start

The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine.

The two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban, portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis.

Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low.

Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is important not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair.

Closer economic cooperation

During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation.

Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar (left) and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy laid wreaths and flowers at a ceremony commemorating the Ukrainian defenders who fell during the Russian invasionImage: Janos Nemes/MTI/AP Photo/picture alliance

The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of new border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv.

Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday.

At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive issues between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a new EU loan for Ukraine.

Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord.

Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part.

Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest.

A fresh — but not always smooth — start

One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation."

Even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth.

Posters belonging to Viktor Orban's Fidesz party portrayed Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Peter Magyar and Ursula von der Leyen as a risk and Fidesz as 'the better choice' in the run-up to the parliamentary election in AprilImage: Martin Fejer/estost.net/EST&OST/IMAGO

In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory.

Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.

Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia.

Hungarian attitudes to Ukraine

Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public.

According to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec, 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine.

That's why Olena Halushka, a Ukrainian political scientist at the International Centre for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV), sees some aspects of Magyar's visit as a concession to public opinion in Hungary.

A monument to members of the military killed during Russia's war in Ukraine in the city of Berehove, the political and cultural center of Ukraine's Hungarian minorityImage: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

"Magyar has taken over a deeply polarized country," she told DW's Ukrainian Service. "A visit to Transcarpathia is more of a step for the Hungarian population than for Ukraine."

Ukraine accommodated not only Magyar's choice of location but also Hungary's demands for better protection of minority rights, which were set out in a 10-point plan in June. That's because EU integration is one of the country's top political priorities.

After planned restrictions on the use of minority languages were withdrawn in late 2023, Ukraine's parliament in early October passed a law on minority language rights that in some respects goes even further than European standards.

Hungary subsequently dropped its obstruction of the opening of negotiating clusters for Ukraine's EU accession.

'Historic' meeting

Laszlo Zubanics, chairman of the Hungarian Democratic Federation in Ukraine (UMDSZ, one of two Hungarian political parties in Transcarpathia), told DW that the Magyar-Zelenskyy meeting was "historic."

He particularly welcomed the fact that Ukraine will probably implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights "not only by the end of 2027, but much sooner, within just a few months."

Laszlo Zubanics welcomed the fact that Ukraine is likely to implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights 'within just a few months'Image: Hanna Sokolova-Stekh/DW

A Hungarian diplomat who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity also called the meeting "historic," adding that after the Orban government's anti-Ukrainian policies, trust now needs to be rebuilt, and that personal meetings between the two leaders play an important role in that process.

The diplomat went on to say that Hungary not only wants to ensure that the rights of the Hungarian minority are protected, it also has a strong interest in being involved in Ukraine's reconstruction.

Overall, the diplomat concluded, both sides are very keen to expand economic cooperation.

A path forward

Hungarian political scientist Daniel Hegedus of the Institute for European Politics (IEP) in Berlin told DW that while the meeting was a "symbolic milestone," it will be important to see "how the two political leaders capitalize on the symbolic political capital generated by this meeting."

No observers have suggested that this is the grand finale of reconciliation between Hungary and Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Tuesday's reset sends an important signal to Europe, namely that if the political will is there, a deep gulf that has existed for years can be transformed into a set of diverging interests that can be addressed through negotiations.

Or, as Zelenskyy put it, now there are "all the opportunities to build hopefully constructive relations."

This article was originally published in German.

items.title: US Army detonates toxic explosives in Iowa despite contamination fears
items.summary: Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the operation was "a huge success".
items.body:

US Army detonates toxic explosives in Iowa despite contamination fears

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said the operation was "a huge success".

The US Army detonates a degraded stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, US, Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Jim Urquhart)

Read a summary of this article on FAST.

Click here to return to FAST

FAST

WASHINGTON: The US Army detonated a massive cache of toxic explosives stored in a tiny Iowa farming town Wednesday (Nov 25), saying the materials were too unstable to move to a safer area and warning residents to shelter from the blast and a potential cloud of lead dust.

Officials said the 68 drums of lead azide - the entire US stockpile of the degraded material - were at risk of spontaneous explosion, requiring their destruction at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, where they had been stored for more than 15 years.

Measures were put in place to curb potential contamination from the destruction of the nearly five tons of explosive material, but the Army encouraged residents of Middletown, Iowa and other nearby areas to leave prior to the blast "out of an abundance of caution".

The controlled explosion sent debris flying into the air and a large cloud of smoke over a tree line, while a New York Times reporter said the blast could be heard some 10 miles (15km) away.

US President Donald Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that "early reports from Iowa are that the Army's mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations".

US Army Acting Secretary Adam Telle speaks at a press conference with other representatives from the military and federal government in Middletown, Iowa, US, Nov 24, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Jim Urquhart)

Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on X that the operation was "a HUGE success."

"We are watching EPA's MASSIVE sensor array throughout the area closely, and there are no readings so far above 0.0," Telle said, referring to the Environmental Protection Agency.

EPA chief Lee Zeldin said on CNN that sampling showed there was "no detection" of lead for now.

The detonation of the explosives was initially scheduled for Nov 20 but was postponed for three days, after which Trump paused the operation pending a court decision and approval from the state's incoming governor, Rob Sand.

"EXTENSIVE PROTECTIVE WORKS"

The court cleared the way for the detonation in a ruling on Monday evening, while Sand said the same day that the "administration should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago".

Colonel Aaron Teller, who led the explosives experts who carried out the detonation, said the last major disposal of lead azide occurred in 1977, when some 7,000 pounds of the substance were destroyed in an open-air blast in Colorado.

Teller said in that case, 75 per cent of the lead particulate remained at the site even with no mitigation measures, and that steps were taken to better contain it in the Iowa detonation.

"There's extensive protective works around those two bunkers, earthen-filled barriers that extend well above the tops of those magazines," Teller told journalists ahead of the detonation.

There was also a vent in the protective works designed to send material released by the blast into an uninhabited area on the grounds of the ammunition plant.

Large water tanks were installed at the site to contain the explosion and keep lead particulate from entering the atmosphere, Teller said, while the Army also sought to curb the blast and the material it released by flooding the exterior of the magazines with a foam material.

Army personnel and local emergency management check in with residents in Middletown, Iowa, US, Nov 25, 2026. (Photo: REUTERS/Jim Urquhart)

The Army released two maps on Wednesday, one showing potential exposure to toxic lead dust in the air in an area extending more than 75 miles (120km) southwest of the blast site, and another picturing possible exposure on surfaces in a more limited area.

"Consider avoiding the highlighted area or remain indoors with windows/doors closed," the maps said, warning that "children under six are especially vulnerable to lead exposure".

The Army also urged a local evacuation prior to the detonation, saying the Federal Emergency Management Agency was "supporting the recommended relocation for all residents of Middletown, Iowa, and immediate surrounding impacted areas".

"Evacuated individuals will be notified by phone once the all-clear is given and at that point may return home," the Army said.

JERUSALEM: Israel's new parliament on Wednesday (Nov 25) took a first step to set up a state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to Hamas's unprecedented Oct 7, 2023 attack, a move long opposed by caretaker Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

On the election campaign trail, centrist prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot had pledged to swiftly establish an independent state commission into the failures that allowed Hamas's attack which resulted in the deaths of more than 1,200 people.

Netanyahu, who was in office during the attack and had long billed himself as the guarantor of Israel's security, had rejected calls to set up such a probe which would have broad investigative powers, instead proposing a commission with members appointed by politicians.

In a preliminary reading in the new parliament formed after Oct 27 elections, 65 members voted in favour of the commission bill put forward by a lawmaker from Eisenkot's party, with 50 against.

The bill will now head to a committee in the Knesset, Israel's parliament, and will have to pass through three further readings before becoming law.

A statement from the Knesset detailing the bill said that the commission would consist of five members and would be required to publish an interim report within one year of the announcement of its establishment.

The bill allocates a budget of seven million shekels (about US$2 million) for the commission's creation.

"SETTING THINGS RIGHT"

Eisenkot's Yashar party described the legislation as "essential to uncovering the truth and drawing the lessons needed to safeguard Israel's security".

"This is the beginning of a process of setting things right for all Israeli citizens," said Yashar member of parliament Orit Farkash-Hacohen, who submitted the bill.

"We must ensure that what happened on that terrible day never happens again."

Transportation Minister Miri Regev, a member of Netanyahu's Likud party, accused the bill's proponents of seeking to target individuals rather than get to the truth.

"They want to investigate our brave and heroic soldiers. They do not want to get to the truth," she said in the Knesset.

Polls have shown broad Israeli support for an independent probe into the deadliest day in the country's history, which inflicted a profound national trauma whose repercussions continue to be felt.

NEW PARLIAMENT

The opposition bloc's legislative offensive follows last week's election of Matan Kahana, a close ally of Eisenkot, as speaker of the Knesset - a strategic position that allows him to expedite or delay debates and votes on proposed legislation.

In the wake of Kahana's election, a committee responsible for organising parliamentary business decided to fast-track consideration of several bills, exempting them from the usual 45-day waiting period.

Eisenkot intends to take advantage of the accelerated procedure to pass several pieces of legislation before even forming a government.

The former general has vowed to reverse several controversial measures adopted under Netanyahu's government, including a judicial overhaul that sparked one of the largest waves of protests in Israel's history.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu obtained a clear majority in the election. Eisenkot was tapped on November 8 to form a new government within 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension.

Avigdor Liberman, a right-wing ally of Eisenkot, said that a government could be presented by the end of next week.

Liberman has opposed relying on lawmakers from Israeli-Arab parties, which posted unprecedented gains on the back of anger over Netanyahu's government.

The left-leaning Democrats, who support inclusion of the Arab minority, on Tuesday halted talks with Eisenkot, voicing alarm over his negotiations with Netanyahu's Likud Party on a coalition.

But the talks on a unity government have made little apparent progress and some observers saw the Democrats' move as tactical as the party jockeys for influence in the next government.

NEW YORK: The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq retreated on Wednesday (Nov 25) amid a tech selloff, but finished well off the day's lows as bargain hunters stepped in ahead of the US Thanksgiving holiday.

The Dow finished higher.

The Nasdaq had been more than 4 per cent lower earlier in the session as the selloff in AI-related stocks and new US tariff proposals hit sentiment.

"There are all these potential headwinds, but then there's also a certain amount of conditioning of buying on the dip, and that's part of what we're seeing," said Oliver Pursche, senior vice president and adviser for Wealthspire Advisors in Westport, Connecticut.

"The broad selloffs tend to kind of throw the baby out with the bathwater. Investors are taking advantage of some of those discrepancies," he said.

Volume was lower than average ahead of the holiday. The market will be closed on Thursday and will close early on Friday.

According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 18.01 points, or 0.25 per cent, to end at 7,183.08 points, while the Nasdaq Composite lost 154.10 points, or 0.65 per cent, to 23,579.44. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 155.20 points, or 0.31 per cent, to 50,173.90.

AI WORRIES WEIGH ON MARKET

Investors were also digesting news that the US proposed new tariffs on goods from 14 trading partners to combat what it calls structural excess industrial capacity, reviving global trade tensions.

Data showed the US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027.

Switzerland 'regrets' closure of diplomatic office in North Korea

"The FDFA regrets this decision and is arranging for the head of the office to return to the embassy of Switzerland in Beijing," the foreign ministry said in a statement.

Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis holds a talk with North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui at Pyongyang Assembly Hall in Pyongyang, Friday, Oct 30, 2026. (Photo: AP/Korean Central News Agency)

GENEVA: Switzerland said Wednesday (Nov 25) it regretted North Korea's sudden closure of its newly opened diplomatic office in Pyongyang in a spat over sanctions.

North Korea's foreign ministry ordered Switzerland's representative to leave within 48 hours and called for the office's closure, state media said.

The Swiss foreign ministry said it regretted the decision but insisted that the closure of the office would not call into question diplomatic relations between the two countries.

Switzerland is one of the few Western nations to maintain dialogue with Pyongyang, and the rebuke comes just weeks after Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis made a rare visit to North Korea, where he officially opened the office and discussed normalising relations.

On Nov 4, following the European Union and Britain, Switzerland imposed sanctions on a camp in the North Korean city of Wonsan, attended by Chinese and Russian children.

The Songdowon International Children's Camp has been accused of helping to indoctrinate Ukrainian children brought from Russian-occupied territories.

The Federal Department of Foreign Affairs said it was informed earlier Wednesday "of the decision by the North Korean authorities to close the Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang".

"The FDFA regrets this decision and is arranging for the head of the office to return to the embassy of Switzerland in Beijing," the foreign ministry said in a statement.

"The reopening of the office in Pyongyang was part of Switzerland's universalist foreign policy.

"This policy aims, in particular, to maintain channels of dialogue with all states, including those with which Switzerland has differences on certain issues."

North Korea leader highlights 'sovereignty' in ties after Trump no-show

The FDFA said Switzerland distinguishes between its sanctions policy and its commitment to maintaining dialogue with all countries.

"The reopening of the office in Pyongyang did not in any way affect Switzerland's implementation of UN sanctions related to North Korea's nuclear programme, nor its implementation of EU sanctions targeting North Korea in the context of Russia's war against Ukraine."

The FDFA said relations would be maintained through the North Korean embassy in Bern, and the Swiss embassy in Beijing, which covers North Korea.

"The closure of the office does not call into question diplomatic relations between Switzerland and North Korea," it said.

Switzerland first established diplomatic relations with North Korea in 1974.

It opened a cooperation office in Pyongyang in 1997.

Before Cassis's visit, the last trip to North Korea by a Swiss government minister was in 2003

items.title: Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
items.summary: A review of the US president's financial disclosures shows Donald Trump's investment portfolios have regularly traded shares in the tech giant.
items.body:
Image source, Reuters

ByThomas Copeland and Alison Benjamin, BBC Verify

Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.

Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.

The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.

The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.

But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.

Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".

Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.

However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.

Image source, Getty Images

Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.

The firm now represents more than 6% of the S&P 500 share index, according to State Street financial services. This makes it the second most valuable company on the index after Apple, whose shares Trump's accounts also frequently trade.

Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.

Our analysis of Trump's Nvidia trades does not include other investment products held by him which may include its shares.

Trump made at least $2.2bn (£1.7bn) from a variety of investments and commercial activities, according to the financial disclosure report for the first year of Trump's second term.

Barbara Perry, a presidential historian at the University of Virginia's Miller Center, told the BBC there is "no precedent for this," adding: "It's beyond anything we've ever seen in the presidency."

Nvidia's chip technology and investments have been critical to the growth of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry, leading to it becoming one of the world's most valuable companies.

Nvidia also ranks highly in many global indices, meaning that investment accounts held around the world, including pensions, are likely to include its shares.

items.title: Nigeria's upcoming election marred by rising AI disinformation
items.summary: As Nigeria inches closer to the 2027 polls, the use of artificial intelligence in the electoral process has prompted questions about integrity and institutional readiness. Can Nigerians trust their democratic processes?
items.body:

Nigeria has just over two months to go until its general election, with incumbent Bola Tinubu running on a ticket focused on combating raging insecurity and resolving the nation's economic crisis. He faces off against former Vice President Atiku Abubakar and senior opposition figure Peter Obi.

The country's electoral body, the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), recently released its preliminary voter's register, which reportedly is riddled with images believed to have been generated using artificial intelligence (AI).

Among the telltale signs of AI usage were exaggerated facial features in images and inconsistencies on the electoral registers, such as duplicates of names and even identities of people who since the previous election had died.

The development raises concerns about the body's overall preparedness ahead of the country's upcoming 2027 general election. Instead of making the upcoming vote more transparent by allowing access to its procedures, INEC has come under fire amid broader controversies about the expanding influence of AI in elections across the continent.

Is Nigeria becoming a one-party state?

Fake news: Nothing new in Nigeria

Joash Amupitan, the chairman of the electoral commission, said the body is now investigating the development, focusing on discrepancies potentially created by AI use.

To this end, he announced the establishment of a dedicated unit to monitor AI-related threats, detect deepfakes and strengthen the integrity of the electoral process, warning that the credibility of the upcoming election could otherwise be under attack.

Supporters of a particular candidate in the election can be easily manipulated to believe AI-driven fake newsImage: Sani Maikatanga/AP Photo/picture alliance

However, even prior to the proliferation of AI across Africa and the globe, this would not be the first time that Nigeria has found itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the circulation of fabricated images, doctored audio and fake videos online. In the run-up to the 2023 election, deepfakes falsely linking candidates to terror-related activities filled social media platforms.

These are often designed to promote certain candidates or to discredit opponents in a bid to influence public perception, which now with the use of AI could create disinformation campaigns of new proportions.

Artificial intelligence has various effects on voter behavior

Lois Ugbede, the assistant editor at the factchecking platform DUBAWA, told DW that "based on our monitoring so far, AI-driven disinformation is serious and is becoming commonplace."

"This could influence political discourse and voter behavior ahead of 2027 because we are already seeing parties using inflated crowds to show that they have a large followership or support," she added.

Have some elections become an empty ritual?

At the same time, rather than influencing the vote in favor of any particular candidate, "the deeper danger is that people may begin to doubt authentic information simply because they know convincing AI-generated fakes are possible," said Akintunde Babatunde, executive director of the Abuja-based Centre for Journalism, Innovation and Development.

"We often focus on the risk of people believing an AI-generated falsehood, but there is another problem where genuine evidence can be dismissed as AI-generated," he noted, citing instances of a lawmaker who recently made inflammatory remarks during a campaign rally — but then claimed the clips were manipulated.

Further pitfalls behind a lack of safeguards against AI

Chibuike Mgbeahuruike, an election consultant at the Centre for Democracy and Development, told DW that apart from the spread of synthetic content online, AI intrusion into the electoral commission's portal could also "undermine its institutional credibility, especially with the low level of confidence that we are already witnessing."

He added, however, that AI itself is not inherently a threat to electoral integrity. The real threat lies in "the absence of effective accountability for its deployment," as innovations in tech increasingly appear to infiltrate governments and their democratic processes.

"Voters must have confidence … that the technology is also transparent, accountable and independently scrutinized, and ultimately subject to human and institutional oversight," said Mgbeahuruike.

Journalists can be just as susceptible to disinformation created by AI and other technologiesImage: Emmanuel Osodi/AA/picture alliance

Mallam Jibrin Baba Ndace, the director-general of state-owned broadcaster Voice of Nigeria, agrees, urging journalists at a recent conference also to not fall into the trap of believing reports, which later could turn out to be false due to AI manipulation.

He stressed the importance of protection measures and due diligence in news media, with the growing inability of public institutions like INEC to provide impartial information due to the use and influence of AI and other election-related tech.

Nigeria's marred relationship with new tech

Beyond AI, Nigeria's electoral processes have undergone various technological shifts over the years in hopes of improving transparency while increasing efficiency.

Electoral authorities first deployed electronic assistance in 2011, when Direct Data Capture Machines were introduced; the devices collect voters' biometrics by scanning fingerprints or capturing facial recognition data with webcams to stop voters from submitting multiple ballots.

Ten years later, a system called the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) was introduced as the new standard, designed to combine fingerprints with facial recognition. However, during the 2023 general election, this voting process was marred by system failures, as poor cell signals delayed these voter accreditation procedures.

Nigeria's voting procedures have increasingly been digitalized since 2011Image: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP

However, with INEC tallying more than 103 million Nigerians registered to participate in the coming poll, disinformation, fake news and technological challenges amount to only a few of several concerns pertaining to Nigeria's democracy.

Voter apathy has become a particular concern, especially among the country's youth. The 2023 election recorded the lowest voter turnout since the country's return to democratic rule in 1999, with merely 27% of registered voters going to the polls.

items.title: Five Russian military jets hit in airfield strike, says Ukraine
items.summary: The Savasleyka airfield hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs at Ukraine.
items.body:
Image source, Getty Images

Image caption,

A Russian MiG-31 military jet (file photo)

ByLaura Gozzi

Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow.

Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield.

Russia has not commented on the strikes.

The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs.

The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down.

Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity.

"Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said.

Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said.

Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia.

"Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes.

Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.

On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities.

But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv.

Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

items.title: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
items.summary: The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.
items.body:
Global Health

How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia

November 25, 20269:14 AM ET

Ari Daniel

Yvonne Capehart Weah's family routinely gets together in the township where she grew up in Liberia. In early November every year, they gather to celebrate the Liberian version of Thanksgiving.

Eddie Raynes

hide caption

Eddie Raynes

Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.

"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."

Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.

That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.

A sacred day for all

Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff, a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving. "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."

When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.

"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.

Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.

"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."

The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.

Yvonne Capehart Weah's nieces and nephews fill their plates at a family gathering in Caldwell.

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

hide caption

Rebecca Blapoh Weah

"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."

(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")

"I'm thanking God"

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."

Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation, an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.

"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

items.title: Why Indian nationals are still ending up in Russia's war on Ukraine
items.summary: Whether through deception or desperation, Indians continue to be drawn into Russia's war in Ukraine. What can New Delhi do to protect its citizens from ending up fighting in Ukraine?
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PsHR

Prefer DW on Google

Modi raised Russian recruitment of Indians when they met in Moscow in July 2024 [FILE]Image: Alexander Zemlianichenko/AP Photo/picture alliance

Advertisement

Gurpreet Singh Randhawa, a 40-year-old from Jalandhar in India's northern Punjab state, said he traveled to Russia for work after responding to a Facebook advertisement for a driving job at a garment factory.

But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces.

After escaping from his unit, he surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November. He is now being held as a prisoner of war.

In an interview with Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin, Randhawa described how, after arriving in Russia, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract and sent for training. He said they confiscated his passport and phone. His account has not been independently verified.

Randhawa's story is a familiar one in India.

He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military. Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces in October 2025. He had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release.

Ukraine war: Plight of Indians trapped in Russian army

India's efforts to bring recruits home

The cases underline how little has changed since Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow in July 2024.

At the time, Putin assured him that Indians who were misled into joining the Russian army would be discharged. But the recruitment of Indians has continued.

In an October filing before the Supreme Court, India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said approximately 267 Indians have joined the Russian armed forces since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Of these, 139 were discharged and 51 were killed. The whereabouts of the 77 others were unknown. Russian authorities have confirmed that seven of them are missing.

The problem extends beyond Indians who travel to Russia seeking civilian employment, only to find themselves exposed to recruitment networks and the dangers of a war zone.

The MEA has also highlighted cases of Indians knowingly enlisting in the Russian military for the supposed financial benefits on offer, believing they could later secure release through government intervention.

Some had also approached Indian authorities to renounce their citizenship and obtain Russian passports. "This is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government," the ministry said.

Lured into war: Russia's foreign fighters in Ukraine

Duped or desperate?

Former diplomat Anil Trigunayat said the growing movement of Indian workers to Russia presents both economic opportunities and new challenges for their protection.

"Inadequate oversight of recruitment networks could leave vulnerable workers exposed to exploitation," Trigunayat told DW.

He said Indian workers were often burdened by substantial recruitment fees and continued deductions from their salaries by intermediaries.

"Some of them had paid between 300,000 to 500,000 Indian rupees [$5,400 /€4,900] to Indian recruitment agents, and even while working in Russia, more than 30% of their agreed monthly salary was taken away by local and foreign agents," Trigunayat said.

The former diplomat added that some Indians who had overstayed their visas in Russia were particularly vulnerable. Military service was allegedly offered to earn substantial wages and regularize their immigration status.

Mohammad Sufiyan, from Hyderabad in the southern state of Telangana, said he was lured to Russia under false pretences and forced into active combat in Ukraine.

He had traveled abroad in search of employment and a better livelihood, but ended up in a war zone. He has since returned home to India.

"Many people are duped. Some decide it is better to seek citizenship than come back to India. It's a tough life, and people will go to any lengths to get some sort of employment," Sufiyan told DW.

Sufiyan's experience points to the economic desperation that makes such offers attractive, even when they carry the risk of being caught up in a war.

Rajan Kumar, a professor at the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of International Studies, said some Indians who traveled to Russia for work could find themselves caught up in the fighting without having joined the military.

"Some of them, they don't join the army, but they end up in the army region. They're caught in the crossfire," Kumar told DW.

He said India was negotiating with Moscow to secure the return of its citizens caught up in such situations. "Russia is very cooperative so far," he said.

India's special relationship with Russia explained

Moscow prioritizes military aims over strategic diplomacy

India has been pressing Russia to take action, but the issue persists.

The recruitment efforts reflect Russia's need for more manpower for its nearly five-year war in Ukraine , and the limited influence New Delhi can exert over Moscow, despite the close political relationship between the two countries.

Mohsin Raza Khan, a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, told DW that Putin's need to sustain the war effort was taking precedence over the concerns of a strategic partner.

He points out that the Russian president was reluctant to impose another mobilization on his own population for fear of domestic unrest.

"In these circumstances, sustaining the war effort appears to take precedence over concerns raised by India. Neither Modi nor New Delhi has sufficient leverage to change that," said Khan.

Khan also said the willingness of some Indians to enlist, and even consider giving up their citizenship, is down to the lack of decent employment opportunities at home.

"For young, educated men without contacts or connections, the chances of respectable employment are so low that the risks of a high casualty war are preferable," he said.

items.title: In Afghanistan, no female doctor often means no treatment for women
items.summary: Millions of women in Afghanistan, particularly pregnant women, are suffering under Taliban restrictions and are increasingly losing access to life-saving medical care.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PrtV

Prefer DW on Google

The UN has been training women as midwives to work in local communities [FILE 2023]Image: Ali Khara/REUTERS

Advertisement

In many parts of Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, male doctors are no longer allowed to treat women. The consequences have been highlighted in a recent United Nations report, which offers disturbing insight into the harsh reality many women face.

In one case, a woman from Kunar province described how she suffered several miscarriages without being able to access medical care.

Her case highlights the increasing number of pregnant women who urgently need medical assistance and are unable to receive it because of restrictions imposed by the Taliban.

And overall, women in Afghanistan are increasingly losing access to essential healthcare. This is due both to the Taliban's restrictions and to cuts in international aid funding.

Taliban remove women from public life in Afghanistan

"If a pregnant woman dies because male doctors are not allowed to treat her, her husband can marry another, younger woman. That is how the Taliban think," said 28-year-old Tamana Zaryab Paryani.

Paryani is an Afghan women's rights activist and one of the best-known voices of resistance against the Taliban.

'Don't send us back': Afghan women in India fear deportation

A trained lawyer, she worked as a newspaper journalist before the Taliban returned to power. Following their takeover in August 2021, she took part in protests against restrictions on the rights of women and girls. In January 2022, she was detained by the Taliban in Kabul alongside her sisters. After her release, she managed to reach Europe.

Since then, she has continued to advocate internationally for the rights of Afghan women. At the end of October, she addressed the UN Security Council, describing the repression of women in Afghanistan and urging the international community not to normalise their systematic disenfranchisement.

"This is gender apartheid. We expect the international community to recognise it and stand with the women of Afghanistan," Paryani told DW.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees severely restricting the lives of women and girls. Girls are barred from secondary education, while women are denied access to universities. Women's opportunities to work outside the home are also severely restricted.

In Afghanistan, girls study in secret to skirt Taliban ban

The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), which monitors and regularly documents the human rights situation in the country, reported in September 2025 that inspectors from the Taliban's Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice were further restricting women's access to healthcare through the enforcement of regulations and decrees.

According to the UN, around 2.6 million girls are excluded from secondary education. This is likely to lead to more girls being married off at an early age and to an increase in maternal mortality, UN Women warns.

Afghanistan has a population of around 45 million. With a median age of approximately 17, it has one of the youngest populations in the world. Around 42% of its population is under the age of 15.

The world's 'worst women's rights crisis'

"What is happening in Afghanistan goes beyond gender-based persecution, as already defined under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court," Haroon Mutasem, professor of International Criminal Law at the American University of Afghanistan and research fellow at Berlin's Humboldt University, told DW.

The Afghan legal scholar examines how the systematic oppression of women in Afghanistan can be classified and prosecuted under international law.

"This is not just about individual acts of persecution, but about an institutionalised system of oppression and domination of one gender group by another. They have established a system that considers women as secondary and defines a life for them as raising kids, working at home, and also actually satisfying the sexual desires of their men."

Mutasem argues that failure to respond to the systematic oppression of Afghan women could undermine the universal validity of human and women's rights. He warns that other authoritarian regimes and extremist movements could adopt similar practices.

According to UN estimates, in 2027 more than 4 million children under the age of five, as well as around 1.27 million pregnant and breastfeeding women, will require treatment for acute malnutrition.

Susan Ferguson, the UN's Special Representative in Afghanistan, described the situation in her latest report as "the world's worst women's rights crisis." Afghan women, she said, are now "fighting for their very survival."

Cuts in aid funding have forced humanitarian organisations to make "impossible decisions about which women and girls can receive support and which have to be turned away," Ferguson said.

Exiled Afghanistan envoy still advocating for women's rights

Army to detonate tons of lead azide after delays. And, Abrego Garcia leaves U.S.

November 25, 20267:18 AM ET

By

Brittney Melton

Army Explosives Detonation In Iowa, Abrego Garcia Leaves The US, Congress And Nvidia

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

The Army will detonate a huge explosion in Middletown, Iowa, this morning to safely dispose of thousands of pounds of lead azide that could spontaneously explode. The explosive has been used since WWI and was moved to the Iowa bunker 17 years ago. The detonation is happening after officials found that the lead azide had crystallized and become unstable. Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.

A sign hangs from a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, on Nov. 23, 2026, in Middletown, Iowa.

Scott Olson/Getty Images

hide caption

Scott Olson/Getty Images

• 🎧 The U.S. Army rescheduled the detonation multiple times after the public got wind of it last week, NPR's Quil Lawrence tells Up First. Purdue University's Andrew Whelton, who has worked on disaster planning, tells Lawrence the detonation caused stress for residents, businesses and farmers. The Trump administration pushed back on the notion that this planned action was a surprise, citing town hall meetings on the topic. Lawrence says the biggest danger in the detonation is to kids and pregnant people due to the lead dust in the air or on surfaces. There are also worries about potential harm to livestock and crops, as well as the cleanup duration.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.

• 🎧 Abrego Garcia's attorney said that he will essentially spend two years waiting abroad. His case raises concerns about due process and the risks of sending individuals to countries where they could be harmed, NPR's Juliana Kim says. The Department of Homeland Security said they are delighted by his decision to leave the U.S. The agency, in a statement, said that "now this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocents." After being mistakenly deported, upon his return to the U.S., Abrego Garcia was charged with human smuggling, an allegation he has denied.

Nvidia's newly reinstated CEO, Jensen Huang, apologized to his staff yesterday for his previous behavior, according to the New York Times. He reportedly denied that Trump pressured the board for his return, despite the president saying otherwise. Huang had stepped down following reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected by U.S. intelligence agencies of being recruited by China's spy agency. Some members of Congress still have concerns about the national security scandal.

• 🎧 Some lawmakers are upset with Huang, while others criticized Nvidia and its board, NPR's Maham Javaid says. Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Tom Cotton of Arkansas is calling for a congressional investigation into Huang and urging faster action on chip-control legislation. House Democratic Committee leaders sent a letter to the president after he claimed he helped with Huang's reinstatement. They asked if he prioritizes friends and allies over the nation's economic and national security interests. They demanded a response by Dec. 8 on what he knew about Huang's ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Huang will attend a closed-door hearing with House members next week, followed by testimony before a Senate committee two days later.

Today's listen

Tatyana Alanis for NPR

NPR launched the first-ever Senior Podcast Challenge this fall, inviting people over 65 to share their stories. Unlike the NPR Student Podcast Challenge, which has attracted more than 90,000 young voices since 2018, this contest focuses on the wisdom and experiences of older voices. While the contest is still open for a few more days, the judges have already listened to more than 100 submissions. Some stories explore life after retirement, dating after divorce or the loss of a partner, and coming to terms with being a senior. Take a listen to some of their favorite early entries.

There's still time to enter. The competition will close on Nov. 30. These are the official rules for the 2026 NPR Senior Podcast Challenge and you can submit your entry here.

Life advice

Beck Harlan for NPR

If you're spending your free time ruminating about work-related issues, you're essentially still on the clock, according to psychologist and author Guy Winch. Don't let workplace woes invade your home life. Winch shares techniques with Life Kit to help you reclaim your time, energy and attention when work consumes too much of your mental bandwidth.

• 🧠 Instead of reliving the work issue, spend 15 minutes creating a plan to address the situation. Ask yourself, "How can I handle this? What outcome do I want?"

• 🧠 Adopt rituals that engage as many senses as possible to help your brain transition between tasks. For example, try changing your clothes to signal the end of the workday. The more you repeat rituals, the easier it is for your brain to shift from work to relaxation.

• 🧠 Do something that energizes you. Activities like screen time and doomscrolling may seem relaxing, but they aren't effective.

• 🧠 Ask yourself: "If my job disappeared tomorrow, what remains of me?" You might realize your worth isn't tied to your job title.

For more guidance on how to switch off your work brain, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

Ezra Frech of Team United States competes during the Men's Long Jump T63 Final on three of the World Para Athletics Championships New Delhi 2025 at Jawaharlal Nehru Stadium on Sept. 29, 2025 in New Delhi, India.

Kenta Harada/Getty Images

hide caption

Kenta Harada/Getty Images

1. Dancing with the Stars wrapped up Season 35 last night, crowning Paralympian Ezra Frech and his partner, Daniella Karagach, as the winners of this year's Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy.

2. Frailejon, a plant of Colombia's high-mountain wetlands that's vital to the country's water supply, is facing an array of threats from farmers, ranchers and climate change. Volunteers are working to save these plants, one seedling at a time.

3. Doctors are combating disinformation about routine vitamin K shots for newborns, which prevent rare but life-threatening hemorrhaging. The rate of parents skipping these shots for their kids has increased from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025, according to new research in JAMA.

Authorities have evacuated a 5-mile radius, and those within 20 miles are advised to stay indoors to avoid exposure to toxins.

The Trump administration pushed back on the notion that this planned action was a surprise, citing town hall meetings on the topic. blocks.text: Kilmar Abrego Garcia has voluntarily left the U.S. after a nearly two-year legal battle. He is the Salvadoran immigrant who became emblematic of the challenges posed by President Trump's mass deportation campaign. Abrego Garcia was arrested in 2025 and mistakenly deported to El Salvador. He returned to the U.S. but departed for Spain yesterday. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that Abrego Garcia boarded a commercial flight to a destination of his choice and "left the United States a free man." Sandoval-Moshenberg described the move as "a temporary departure," saying that Abrego Garcia, whose wife and child are U.S. citizens, has options to return to the U.S.

items: 🎧 Abrego Garcia's attorney said that he will essentially spend two years waiting abroad. Elizabeth Warren says that Huang owes Congress answers about Nvidia's compliance with laws designed to keep advanced chips out of China. Republican Sen. Congress

Lawmakers seek answers on the national security as Nvidia CEO returns

Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia with President Trump's backing. But the questions surrounding the AI chipmaker and its ties to China are far from settled.

U.S. intelligence officials told congressional staff there is no evidence that Alice Huang, the woman who had an affair with the Nvidia chief, was a Chinese spy or intelligence asset, according to a person familiar with the matter who was granted anonymity to speak about a closed-door briefing.

There is also no evidence that she initiated the affair to collect intelligence for China's government, the person told NPR's Ryan Lucas on condition of anonymity because of the sensitive nature of the matter. She is, however, believed to have passed along information after the affair began.

Trump has said he helped arrange Huang's return as CEO, and Nvidia's board maintains that his reinstatement presents no national security risk. Some Republican lawmakers, however, want to understand how those conclusions were reached.

Speaking to Morning Edition on Wednesday, before NPR obtained the new information, Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., said he wants to hear from the FBI and CIA before Huang appears before House lawmakers next week.

For Fitzpatrick, a former FBI special agent who sits on the House Intelligence Committee, the inquiry begins with what federal authorities knew and whether they warned the Nvidia chief of potential espionage threats.

"What briefings did they give? When did they give them?" he asked.

Huang's reinstatement, Fitzpatrick said, should not put those questions to rest.

"The public is rightly concerned, and they deserve answers," he said.

Fitzpatrick also wants to hear from Attorney General Todd Blanche, who on Tuesday described Nvidia as a good corporate citizen, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose department faces questions over Nvidia's chip exports to China.

"Anytime you do an investigation, you follow the facts wherever they lead, and you report those facts with unimpeachable integrity," Fitzpatrick said. "You leave no stone unturned."

The debate over Huang's reinstatement extends beyond Washington.

In Silicon Valley, his return has alarmed women and advocates who have spent years pushing for a better workplace culture, renewing questions about the limits of executive accountability.

items.title: Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor
items.summary: Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts — from beating sun to freezing nights, fire and snow.
items.body:
Greetings from Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest point in all its splendor

November 25, 20266:00 AM ET

Emily Feng

Emily Feng/NPR

As dawn broke one recent morning over camp, we got one of our first full views of the peak of Mount Kilimanjaro, normally hidden behind clouds.

Climbing tall mountains like Kilimanjaro is a study in contrasts. The beating sun bakes you during the day, walking so close to the equator, but the nights quickly dip below freezing. Snow remains constantly in sight from humid rainforest and alpine landscapes, freshly charred from a wildfire three weeks before. And always beckoning is the peak, within sight, but seemingly never nearer; the high altitude means hikers need to walk slowly or else risk exhaustion and altitude sickness.

A group of friends and fellow hikers and I spent days camping at altitude to acclimatize before a final summit push during our second-to-last evening on the mountain. We trudged through heavy snow under the stars, cresting a massive volcanic crater rim, and leaned against drifts of what had become a full blizzard to reach the top in the early morning hours. I stood on the peak I'd seen only from a distance for the last week but saw only whiteness: all snow and ice, the absence of life and color heightened by my low oxygen levels.

Days later, having descended and decompressed and readying myself to fly back home, I looked back at the mountain one last time. For a few minutes, in the dusk light, the clouds parted and she revealed herself before disappearing again into the darkening evening, still as elusive as ever.

items.title: Fact check: Deepfakes and 'US abandons Taiwan' claims spread ahead of vote
items.summary: Ahead of local elections, Taiwan is seeing a surge in AI-generated attacks on mayoral candidate Puma Shen, alongside disinformation portraying the US as abandoning the island.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PguY

Prefer DW on Google

DPP supporters at a campaign event ahead of Taiwan's local elections, which have seen a rise in online disinformationImage: Cheng Yu-chen/AFP

Advertisement

On November 28, Taiwan will hold local elections that could reshape power dynamics between the sovereignty-leaning Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the Beijing-friendly Kuomintang (KMT). The outcome could influence relations between Taiwan and China, as well as regional geopolitics and ties between Washington, Beijing and Taipei.

A month before the election, there was a spike in AI-generated content featuring DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen. Claims that the US is abandoning Taiwan also increased during the same period. Experts say that fake quotes and misleading clips are being used as part of a campaign to weaken trust in US security commitments.

Did Trump offer to sell US arms to China?

The V-Dem Institute at the University of Gothenburg ranked Taiwan "the country most severely targeted" by foreign disinformation for eleven consecutive years – from 2014 to 2024.

The Taiwanese Ministry of the Interior has stated that foreign actors are increasingly using diverse methods to interfere in elections. That includes manipulating election betting, inviting Taiwanese citizens to China, using donations from Taiwanese business people to organize events, such as banquets, and leveraging temple and religious activities, to mobilize and win over supporters. Taiwan has functioned with de facto independence since 1949 despite Beijing's decadeslong claim to the island as a province and repeated vows to annex it.

DW Fact Check examined viral claims that have circulated online since September during the run-up to the election.

Deepfake audio, video target pro-sovereignty candidate

Claim: Puma Shen takes drug and receives kickbacks through arms purchases from the US.

DW Fact check: Fake

AI-generated audio recordings attacking DPP's Taipei mayoral candidate circulated on Facebook one month before Taiwan's local electionsImage: Facebook

An audio clip posted on Facebook on October 29, claims to show Puma Shen, the DPP candidate for Taipei mayor, admitting to receiving kickbacks from US arms deals.

The recording is heavy with background noise – a method used to mask synthetic manipulation in AI-generated audio. Multiple deepfake detection platforms, including Is this AI and Undetectable, flagged the audio as likely AI-generated.

The Facebook account that posted the audio was created on October 29, 2026 – the date the audio was also published. The account's followers are mainly profiles using languages, such as English, Arabic and Thai. That points to possible bot activity.

Another Facebook account posted an image of Puma Shen taking drugs. Apart from the "AI content" label on the post, multiple AI detector tools identified this photo as likely AI-generated.

Taiwanese independent media platform Watchout discovered that the advertiser behind this Facebook account is located in ChinaImage: Facebook

The account was created in March 2026. Since then, a lot of AI-generated content mocking Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te and his pro-sovereignty party has been posted. It is occasionally interspersed with posts praising the development of Chinese cities.

This account's profile indicates that the primary country location for people who manage this page includes China and Taiwan.

Taiwanese independent media platform Watchout investigated the account's advertising activity and found that it had previously run at least five Facebook ads. The advertisers were identified as Peng Zhiwei and Guo Yang, both based in China. The findings suggest that the account received financial support from individuals in China.

The AI detection tool "AI or Not" indicates that this photo is likely AI-generatedImage: aiornot.com

The Taipei mayoral race is a key battleground in Taiwan's upcoming local elections. As of mid-November, polls showed a neck-and-neck contest between Puma Shen and his opponent, Chiang Wan-an, who claims to be a great-grandson of Taiwanese leader Chiang Kai-shek.

Chiang Kai-shek was a leading figure of the Kuomintang and relocated with the party to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese Civil War to the Chinese Communist Party.

While the Kuomintang was historically staunchly anti-communist, critics argue that it now promotes closer ties with China. For example, they point to a senior Kuomintang figure's proposed 10-year unification framework as evidence that its stance runs counter to mainstream public opinion in Taiwan. Although the Kuomintang subsequently stated that this framework is entirely unrelated to the current party leadership, it has sparked controversy in Taiwan.

Distorted quotes and misleading clips

Claim: A TikTok video claims to show US president Donald Trump saying the US is abandoning Taiwan.

DW Fact check: Misleading

In this TikTok video, Donald Trump's response in an interview was interpreted beyond what the US president had actually saidImage: tiktok.com

The original video was from a Fox News interview with Trump on May 16. The interviewer did not ask whether the United States would defend Taiwan, and the US president did not comment on the issue.

Trump said he did not want Taiwan to become independent or for a war to break out, adding that the status quo should be maintained to allow tensions to de-escalate. He also clearly stated that his policy toward Taiwan "has not changed." Washington has long maintained a policy of strategic ambiguity toward Taiwan– neither explicitly guaranteeing the island's defense nor ruling out the possibility of doing so.

This has been removed because while they were sensational, they were not entirely wrong because they referred to a report by a thinktank. We apologize for the error.

items.title: China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining
items.summary: The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
items.body:
Asia

China investigates Politburo member and Shanghai party chief Chen Jining

November 25, 20264:44 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025.

Ng Han Guan/AP

hide caption

Ng Han Guan/AP

BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.

The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.

Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.

A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.

The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.

The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.

"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."

The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.

"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."

Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.

The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.

Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.
