items.title: Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco
items.summary: Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.
items.body:
Sports

Africa Cup title given back to Senegal after sports court rules against Morocco

November 25, 20261:43 AM ET

By

The Associated Press

FILE - Senegal's Sadio Mane holds the trophy aloft as he celebrates with teammates after winning the Africa Cup of Nations final soccer match between Senegal and Morocco in Rabat, Morocco, Sunday, Jan. 18, 2026.

Youssef Loulidi/AP

hide caption

Youssef Loulidi/AP

More than 10 months on from a chaotic, controversial final, Senegal is Africa's soccer champion once again.

Senegal won back the Africa Cup of Nations title in a legal fight on Tuesday after the Court of Arbitration for Sport overturned an earlier ruling which handed the trophy to Morocco.

Senegal won the Africa Cup on the field in Morocco in January and then lost it in a legal case in March because its players walked off the field in protest in second-half stoppage time.

CAS has now rejected that earlier ruling, based on referee Jean-Jacques Ndala's decision to let the game resume after the protest.

"The Court of Arbitration for Sport has delivered justice to sport," Senegalese soccer federation president Abdoulaye Fall said in a statement.

The legal battle may not be over yet after Morocco announced plans to appeal, likely to Switzerland's supreme court, in a challenge to the integrity of a senior CAS judge.

Tournament regulations said a team which refuses to play should be considered to have lost the game, but CAS said those rules were meant only for cases "when a team's conduct leads the referee to call off the game permanently."

Ndala "did not err in law" when he resumed the game and had "sole authority" to make that call, CAS said, adding its three judges were unanimous.

"The panel acknowledged that the referee had to make a decision in an atmosphere of extreme tension," CAS said. "However, these circumstances do not justify describing the decision as 'arbitrary.' On the contrary, the referee's judgment did not appear to have been affected by factors external to the game."

Morocco raises concerns over CAS process

Morocco's soccer federation detailed plans for an appeal that targets one of the three judges on the CAS panel.

In a statement, the Moroccan federation protested what it described as the court's failure to address potential integrity concerns, alleging "confirmed communication" between German arbitrator Ulrich Haas and Fall, the Senegalese soccer president, 48 hours before the decision was issued.

The CAS director general, Matthieu Reeb, acknowledged to reporters at the court in Lausanne that a Moroccan protest was received just minutes before the verdict was announced.

Reeb said the court's panel "in charge of petitions for challenge has conceded that there was not enough elements at this stage to postpone the notification of the award."

CAS verdicts can be challenged at Switzerland's supreme court, also in Lausanne, though only on limited procedural grounds of which a judge's integrity could be one.

Haas has been among the most respected and in-demand CAS judges in the past 20 years, selected by parties in storied cases involving Manchester City's beating a Champions League ban by UEFA, tennis star Simona Halep's doping case and Africa's Champions League final in 2019.

Patrick Kabou, a lawyer for the Senegalese Soccer Federation, called the alleged communication between Fall and Haas "unreal."

Sports

European nations say World Cup boycott is still on, keeping FIFA's Infantino in limbo

Trouble on the field and in the stands

Senegal won the final 1-0 after extra time with chaos on the field and violent clashes in the stands. Even the ball boys were involved in scuffles as they tried to snatch towels that Senegal goalkeeper Edouard Mendy was using to keep his gloves dry.

The result was overturned two months later as a 3-0 default win for Morocco by an appeals panel appointed by the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

Senegal beat AFCON host nation Morocco after a 15-minute delay in play. At 0-0, Senegal's team walked off the field to protest Morocco being awarded a penalty kick in the last minute of regulation time.

Match referee Ndala of Congo eventually allowed the game to restart, Morocco's penalty by Real Madrid forward Brahim Diaz — a slow chip shot known as a "Panenka" — was saved, and Senegal won in extra time.

The drama continued through the months of legal tussles. Senegal's players paraded with the trophy ahead of a game in March against Peru, even though Morocco was recognized as the champion at that point.

Both teams played at the World Cup believing themselves to be the rightful champion of Africa.

Soccer's laws versus regulations

Senegal had the laws of the game on its side, and Morocco had the tournament regulations.

The laws of soccer state that referee decisions are final. CAS backed that position with its own "field of play" doctrine, that on-field calls by a referee generally can't be taken to the sports court.

"By blowing his whistle to restart play, the referee considered that the conditions for resuming the match had been met — both teams were on the pitch again, and both expressed their willingness to resume," CAS said.

In the first legal case in March, CAF appeal judges cited AFCON tournament regulations that if a team "refuses to play or leaves the ground before the regular end of the match without the authorization of the referee, it shall be considered loser and shall be eliminated for good from the current competition."

The CAS judges heard evidence at a one-day hearing last month and the court promised a verdict by the end of November with a full written ruling of its judges setting out reasons for their decision.

The next men's AFCON starts in June co-hosted by Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania. Morocco will aim to end a wait for the title which now stands at 50 years.

Soccer fans in Senegal celebrate a win

"Senegal won on the pitch, and the court simply confirmed what we all already knew: We are the real champions of Africa," said Mariama Sidibé, 35, an accountant in the capital, Dakar.

Sidibé said the dispute between Morocco and Senegal should now be left in the past.

"With all of this behind us, we should focus on what unites us now, and who knows, maybe Morocco can have its revenge on the field during the next AFCON this summer," she said.

"At the end of the day Morocco and Senegal are brothers," Sidibé added, referring to the countries' long shared close ties built on religion, trade and culture.

Sidi Sylla, a philosophy student at Dakar's main university, said the court's ruling was "not just a win for Senegal but for football in general."

Historic decision

CAS rulings have stripped many athletes of Olympic medals for doping, but it's rare to overturn the result of a major soccer competition.

CAS refused to change the results of the 2019 Asian Cup, dismissing an appeal that the star striker on winning team Qatar shouldn't have been eligible for the tournament.

A lengthy legal battle over the same year's African Champions League final also ended with the original winner, Esperance of Tunisia, taking the title after its opponent Wydad from Morocco refused to play on.

One notable CAS ruling on a team sport title came at the Winter Olympics in 2022. A doping case involving then-15-year-old Russian figure skater Kamila Valieva ended up with her disqualification, and the Russian team being dropped from gold to bronze in the team event.

items.title: Ukraine's bid for NATO membership and more air defense remains controversial
items.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is calling for the rapid acceptance of his country into NATO. However, the necessary unanimity for this is lacking, as shown during the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PnQ4

Prefer DW on Google

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy participated in the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin via video conferenceImage: Liesa Johannssen/REUTERS

Advertisement

It took a while for the video call to connect. When Volodymyr Zelenskyy finally greeted the delegates in Berlin, applause broke out. The Ukrainian president appealed to the gathered parliamentarians from 32 NATO member states to keep supporting his country, especially against the massive aerial bombardment from Russia.

"Dear friends, winter is now ahead of us. And of course, our number one priority is air defense," Zelenskyy told the delegates. His country urgently needs more Patriot and other comprehensive anti-air attack systems. "And your countries have them. Missiles that can stop Russian ballistic missiles should not be sitting in warehouses collecting dust. And we say this openly. Please help us with this."

Western allies boost Ukraine's defenses but clash over deep strikes

Ukraine seeks to join NATO

Zelenskyy renewed his call for his country to join the NATO military alliance. That issue is not for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly, which was gathered for its 72nd annual meeting in Berlin, to decide. But it was important to the Ukrainian president to reiterate his request.

After the war ends, Ukraine needs strong security guarantees and NATO could ensure those. "Wouldn't it be more effective to simply bring Ukraine into NATO?" Zelenskyy asked, arguing: "Wouldn't that be better for all of us, for everyone? Cheaper to put in place? And more reliable when it comes to actually protecting security?"

There is conflict among NATO members about the possibility of admitting Ukraine. The alliance has affirmed multiple times that the path to membership stands open to Ukraine — however, in the long term rather than the near future. This is primarily because of the ongoing war and the possible assistance obligations of other NATO countries for Ukraine, which was attacked by Russia.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte rejected the Ukrainian demands at the summit, which for the first time in 26 years was held in Berlin. Ukraine had entry prospects; however, NATO members currently lack unanimity on this issue. NATO alone decides who becomes a member. "There is total clarity on that within the alliance," Rutte said.

If Russia attacked NATO, would Germany be prepared?

Merz: Denying Ukraine NATO membership in 2008 'was a mistake'

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz advocated for Ukraine to receive security guarantees similar to what NATO members have, in the instance of a possible ceasefire. In retrospect, it was clear "what a mistake it was not to follow the American suggestion back in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest to admit Ukraine as a member," Merz said at a joint press conference following a meeting with Rutte.

Whether or not a NATO entry for Ukraine could be part of negotiations with Russia is another question, according to Rutte. He approved of current US efforts to bring about peace talks, and how Europe was closely consulting with Ukraine and the US for a unified position. "But it is also to test now whether Putin is willing to play ball, and then these issues might come up again."

The Russian invasion of Ukraine has led to NATO arming itself on a massive scale. Members have committed to raising their countries' defense spending to 5% of their gross domestic product (GDP) by 2035.

Rutte warned that all the allies needed a credible path to get there, "and ideally, they get there sooner than 2035." In addition, he said weapons production among member states needed to further increase because "right now, demand still far exceeds the supply."

Why Germany's military ambitions face a battle at home

Germany's military budget has had a massive increase

The contribution by Germany's Bundeswehr armed forces to NATO was explained by Carsten Breuer, Germany's highest-ranking soldier. For example, the massive increase in military spending: "Our defense budget has tripled since 2021. The goal is to achieve the 5% target, which was set at the summit in The Hague, well before 2035." In the coming year, Germany's defense budget has risen to more than €139 billion ($151 billion).

The Bundeswehr was further developing into a "constantly modernized, effective and innovative army, Breuer said. Also, a much larger one than before. "To reach our current capability goals we are expanding the Bundeswehr to a total of 460,000 soldiers by the mid-2030s," the German chief of defense said. Of those, 200,000 are to be reservists. "This is like walking a tightrope because we must find the right balance between growth and operational readiness."

Following his speech, Breuer answered questions from the delegates who showed keen interest in the developments. The discussion was a preview of Breuer's new post: He has been voted in as the new chair of the NATO Military Committee and will move to the alliance's headquarters in Brussels mid-next year. Then he will become the principal military advisor to NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte. "I take this election as a sign of recognition that Germany has now accepted its responsibility as well as its role in security policy," Breuer said.

items.title: EU enlargement: Why do some EU member states use their vetoes to block the accession of certain candidate countries?
items.summary: Individual EU member states use their veto powers to block candidate countries in the accession process — often for reasons of domestic politics. DW takes a look at some cases and examines what's behind them.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PobR

Prefer DW on Google

Will the European Union soon have 28 members or more? Or will some member states block the accession of certain candidate countries?Image: Nicolas Economou/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Advertisement

It's been quite a while since the European Union's last enlargement, when Croatia joined the bloc back in 2013.

If everything goes according to plan, another might soon be on the cards: Montenegro, with a population of just 620,000, could complete accession negotiations in the coming months and join the EU in early 2028.

But no sooner had EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos made this announcement in October than news emerged that Croatia might veto Montenegro's accession unless the country meets a series of Croatian demands. EU politicians and MEPs were dismayed.

This is not the first time something like this has happened: The veto rights that member states have on many EU matters have increasingly been used by individual countries in recent years as a means of leverage or obstruction, paralyzing the EU in the process.

EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in October that Montenegro could become a member of the European Union in 2028Image: Dursun Aydemir/Anadolu/IMAGO

DW takes a look at some of the most significant cases, the background to them and what are — in some instances — the serious political consequences of them.

Montenegro: Croatia's eight demands

Montenegro is the most advanced EU candidate country, with a potential accession date of 2028. It has already provisionally closed several of the EU's 33 negotiating chapters.

As of November 23, however, Croatia is blocking the closure of three chapters that have already been negotiated.

Zagreb is demanding, among other things, compensation for former prisoners held in Montenegrin camps during the Yugoslav wars of the 1990s, clarification of the fate of Croatians who have been missing since that time, and more rigorous prosecution of war crimes.

There are also disputes over the precise maritime boundary between the two countries. In addition, Croatia is demanding payment of about €2.4 billion (about $2.6 billion) for assets that belonged to the Yugoslav People's Army, the army of the former Yugoslavia to which both countries belonged before its breakup in the early 1990s.

Croatia is calling, among other things, for the return of the training ship Jadran, which used to belong to the Yugoslav Royal Navy and was based in Split (now Croatia) before the Yugoslav warsImage: Martin Vas/Depositphotos/IMAGO

Montenegro has already responded to some of Croatia's demands, including those concerning compensation for former prisoners. Others, such as the one relating to the assets of the Yugoslav People's Army, are disputed.

It is clear that Croatia's list of demands is also driven by domestic politics. No government in Zagreb can afford to appear compliant on issues relating to the Croatian War of Independence (1991–95).

Moreover, moderate conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic, who is regularly accused in Croatia of being too pro-EU, can use the dispute to portray himself as a staunch defender of national interests.

Ukraine: Hungarian domestic politics in the name of a minority

After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the EU in June 2022 granted Ukraine and the Republic of Moldova EU candidate status through an accelerated procedure as a gesture of solidarity.

Many EU member states have reservations about Ukraine joining the bloc quickly. Nevertheless, only Hungary, under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban, adopted an obstructive stance.

Ostensibly, Hungary's obstruction was about getting Ukraine to improve the rights of the Hungarian minority in Transcarpathia in western Ukraine. But Orban used the matter for domestic political purposes and as an election campaign issue, portraying Ukraine as a "mafia state."

items.title: Why Iran's medicine supply chain is failing
items.summary: Pharmacies in Iran are closing, hospital deliveries have stalled and patients are rationing doses or turning to black markets.
items.body:
https://p.dw.com/p/5PopQ

Prefer DW on Google

Iran has faced medicine shortages for years. But the current war is making things worse [FILE 2018]Image: Kyodo News/IMAGO

Advertisement

Ahmad,* 67, visited nearly 20 Tehran pharmacies for the antipsychotic drug chlorpromazine, but left empty-handed.

"When a patient has to go to this many pharmacies just to find an essential drug, you really have to ask who is responsible for supplying medicine," he told DW.

Mitra,* a 37-year-old Tehran resident with diabetes , spent days hunting for insulin. "These are not drugs I can postpone taking or simply give up," she said. "My life depends on regular access to this insulin."

Their ordeal reflects a wider crisis across Iran's health care system.

Along with Tehran residents, DW spoke with an official at Iran's Food and Drug Administration (IFDA) and pharmacy workers in Tehran, Rasht and Mahabad. The interviews were conducted anonymously or using pseudonyms as speaking with foreign media remains dangerous in Iran.

Iran's broken drug supply chain

The official said that Iran's falling currency, along with price controls, has drained domestic drugmaker profits, while unpaid hospital debts have delayed deliveries.

"Add our own hospitals' heavy unpaid debts to distributors, and you can see why distribution has ground to a halt and companies are no longer supplying hospitals," the official said.

"Unless the Plan and Budget Organization makes our currency allocation realistic, banks step in with loans for drugmakers and insurers settle their debts, the Health Ministry's hands will remain tied and this disaster cannot be stopped," the official warned.

Some patients are being forced to ration supplies [FILE 2024] Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

IFDA spokesman Mohammad Hashemi told Iran's semi-official ILNA news agency on November 9 that fewer than 40 of roughly 700 essential drugs faced supply difficulties. However, pharmacists told DW about how difficult it can be to get drugs on shelves.

A pharmacy manager in Tehran said insurance payments are often delayed by months, while drug prices continue to climb. Another pharmacist in the northwestern Mahabad region said distributors demand cash upfront for scarce items.

The insurance delays and shifting rules have pushed some pharmacies to drop contracts or refuse costly insured drugs.

The pharmacist in Mahabad, who prefers to be called Leili,* said that general pharmacies can lack about 40 items, and larger specialty pharmacies stocking chemotherapy and complex treatments can lack over 100, including psychiatric and Parkinson's drugs, and insulin vials.

"Many drugs can no longer be found in the official supply chain at all, such as nimodipine tablets [used to treat certain strokes] or hospital injectable antibiotics that have no substitutes," she said.

Turning to low-quality, black market medicine

As common items like cold medication become scarcer or more expensive, some people are turning to home remedies, she said. She added that for essential medicines like insulin, chronic patients are using smaller doses to preserve supply.

Many of those unable to pay are middle-class customers whom pharmacists cannot easily refer to charities, she said, with elderly and psychiatric patients among the hardest hit.

Leili warned that lower quality seen in some reverse-engineered domestic drugs presents a high risk for cancer, transplant and autoimmune patients.

She added that some families are forced to turn to street markets usually located outside of clinics, which lack cold-chain controls and sell counterfeit medicines or drugs with altered expiration dates.

Another pharmacy manager who asked to be called Khadiv* said scarce medicines can fetch up to 10 times their official price.

Sanctions and blockades

Amid the current conflict with the US, Khadiv said US sanctions, along with border disruptions and the US maritime blockade in the Strait of Hormuz inflate import costs.

In a statement, the US State Department told DW its sanctions follow international law to deny Tehran funds for "destabilizing behavior," stressing the measures allow "broad authorizations and exceptions" for food, medicine and medical devices. It pointed to what it called Iran's "corrupt ruling elite" for not properly allocating resources.

Iranian officials, however, reject that claim. In late summer, Health Minister Mohammad Reza Zafarghandi called US exemption claims "a big lie," saying banking, insurance, flight and shipping sanctions block imports.

Earlier this fall, the IFDA's raw materials chief cited currency, banking, customs and shipping hurdles as the main bottleneck.

DW emailed the Iranian Embassy's media office in Berlin for comment but received no reply.

"Seeing so many people unable to afford their medicine or reach medical centers leaves me with a sense of guilt and helplessness," Khadiv said, adding that lack of access can even lead to patient deaths.

For patients like Ahmad and Mitra, the standoff offers no relief, and every day, the gap between official assurances and what is actually on pharmacy shelves grows harder to ignore.

*Names changed for safety reasons.

When sanctions threaten people's health

items.title: Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?
items.summary: Albania's Prime Minister Edi Rama has vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned. But an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.
items.body:
Who really owns the Albanian land Jared Kushner wants to turn into a 5-star resort?

November 24, 20269:24 AM ET

Rob Schmitz

Questions over a Trump family investment in Albania

Listen

·
13:02

13:02

• Download

• Embed

<iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/g-s1-154623/nx-s1-mx-6053109-1" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">

The sun sets over coastal mountains near the city of Vlore, the region where Jared Kushner plans to build a five-star luxury resort. The land that Kushner bought for this project, though, is claimed by several local Albanians and its ownership is being investigated by state prosecutors.

Rob Schmitz/NPR

hide caption

Rob Schmitz/NPR

ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.

And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.

"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."

A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."

Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.

They say it's theirs.

Gentian Mocka says his family has owned this strip of beach, named Hidrovor Beach, since the time of the Ottoman Empire. The land is now slated to be developed for a luxury hotel owned by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump. In the background is Sazan Island, a publicly owned island that Trump and Kushner also say they will develop.

Rob Schmitz/NPR

hide caption

Rob Schmitz/NPR

Land grabs and falsified documents

"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.

After World War II, Albania's Communist government seized it — along with all private land.

When communism fell in 1991, families like Mocka's embarked on a years-long process to get their land back. "But then our problems started with the guys that were much more powerful than we were — had a lot of political support, were very rich and very well connected with the politics of that time," says Mocka.

In 2005, Mocka learned that someone else was laying claim to his family's land — a fellow Albanian named Artur Shehu. It was a familiar name for those who lived here in the 1990s, when the regional capital of Vlore was outside the control of the country's government. It was instead run by mafia-style gangs. At the time, Shehu was well-known to police in Vlore for his alleged involvement in a crime syndicate that, according to Albanian prosecutors, smuggled drugs and migrants into Europe. He fled Albania in 1999, after what police say was a shootout with a rival gang.

He ended up in the United States, where he received asylum in 2001 and, later, became a U.S. citizen. The 60-year-old Shehu now lives in a villa in Miami Beach. But he's continued to manage a growing real estate portfolio back in Albania through an associate in Vlore named Pellumb Petritaj.

The pair has claimed plots of land — including Mocka's family plot — up and down the southern Albanian coast, and prosecutors have taken notice. In 2018, Petritaj served three years in prison for forging land titles on behalf of Shehu. And on Nov. 18, Petritaj was sentenced to another seven years in prison for falsifying documents to $17 million worth of oceanfront property in the city of Vlore on behalf of Shehu. The court ordered the land — which does not include Mocka's family plot — confiscated from Shehu last week. The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.

Albanian prosecutors say land linked to Kushner may have been "illegally acquired"

The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.

The quiet village has only a couple hundred residents. Most of them, like Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota, are past the age of 70. On a recent warm and sunny afternoon, the two are resting on benches in the courtyard of the village church after a day of harvesting olives. They nod their heads when asked about Artur Shehu.

"He is from the village of Kanina, far from here and up in the mountains," says Konomi, motioning inland, "but his family has never lived here. He's involved in shady dealings."

The village of Zvernec, along the Adriatic coast, is at the center of a land dispute involving Jared Kushner. Several of the village's residents say the land that Kushner is claiming is actually theirs.

Rob Schmitz/NPR

hide caption

Rob Schmitz/NPR

Then Kota speaks up. "There wasn't a single soul of that family living here, going back to the Ottoman times," she says. "But we've heard stories about him, and we're very scared of him."

Twenty years ago, Kota, Konomi and dozens of others in this village learned that Artur Shehu had somehow acquired their farmland. They filed suit in Albanian court to reclaim their land, a fight that escalated this past April when Shehu sold the 300-acre parcel that includes what they say is their farmland to a company developing a luxury resort project for Kushner.

That transaction, however, is under review.

In court documents obtained by NPR, Albanian prosecutors argue that the land involved in Kushner's development is "suspected of having been illegally acquired through forgery."

A spokesman for Kushner did not respond to NPR's request for comment by the time this article was published. Kushner had previously issued a statement on his website saying his partnership purchased the land from a private party in a private transaction. "Title was reviewed by counsel and verified," the statement says.

Shehu did not respond to NPR's request for comment. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. However, in Tirana, a former lawyer for Shehu was willing to talk.

Oceanfront properties are now claimed by several parties

"The people that Artur [Shehu] has authorized by power of attorney to deal with his family's properties committed a forgery in which they removed the property from the brother of Artur's grandfather and passed it to Artur's grandfather," says Kujtim Cakrani. "That is the whole story of the property."

Cakrani says Shehu's associates forged an inheritance certificate that made it appear that Shehu's grandfather had owned the land, which was then passed to Artur Shehu himself. And then last April, Shehu sold that land to Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, Syrian-born Qatari billionaire brothers who are financial partners of Jared Kushner.

Cakrani says that when he discovered that Artur Shehu was involved in this alleged forgery, he dropped him as his client. "I could no longer continue representing him because of the seriousness of the matter," he says. "It is impossible for me, with these documents that he has, to defend him."

And this is why, Cakrani says, Albanian state prosecutors have put Shehu under investigation and froze his bank accounts. Cakrani says he is now representing a group of 30 relatives of Shehu who he claims to be the rightful owners of this land.

Kujtim Cakrani is the former lawyer of Artur Shehu, the man who sold the property along Albania's southern coast to a pair of billionaire brothers who represent Jared Kushner. He says he's since dropped Shehu as a client.

Rob Schmitz/NPR

hide caption

Rob Schmitz/NPR

Gentian Mocka, as well as Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota in Zvernec, tell NPR that nobody by the name of Shehu — neither Artur nor his relatives — has any legal claim to what they say is their land, oceanfront property that has now been claimed by several parties, including the son-in-law of the president of the United States.

Wealthy speculators have exploited land in Albania since the fall of communism

Albanian real estate law expert Roden Hoxha says he has seen this kind of land battle many times before. "But now that Kushner is in it," he says, "everybody is freaking out."

He says land ownership in Albania is complicated by decades under a Stalinist regime that stole all the land from private owners and collectivized it. When communism fell in 1991, he says Albania became a land grab free-for-all.

"It was basically chaos," he says. "People started claiming land wherever they threw a stone. It was basically the Albanian version of the U.S.' claiming of the West."

Hoxha describes wealthy speculators keen to exploit the chaos of the moment: locals whose families have farmed the land for generations and well-connected operators like Shehu, who aggressively try to claim that land. "And then on the international level," says Hoxha, most recently, "it exploded because it was Kushner and Trump and Arab money behind it."

And so, Hoxha says, what at first appeared to be yet another Albanian land dispute now has ties all the way to the White House. In the end, an Albanian court will likely decide who the rightful owner of this property is. But for now, it has sparked unprecedented public outrage in Albania. Protesters have taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, every day since May 31, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. But Rama has only vowed to crack down harder on what have become increasingly violent demonstrations against his entire government.

Rama has also vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned, but an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.

When contacted by NPR, Elona Sinaj, Rama's spokesperson, sent a statement saying, "If the seller does not have legitimate ownership of the property, the money will remain within the Republic of Albania, and certainly it will be used for anyone who proves that his claim over the property is grounded."

Sinaj went on to say that the ambition for Rama's government is "to create a new benchmark for sustainable Mediterranean development."

Some Albanians see advantages to having a Kushner-linked resort

That goal aligns with Kushner's vision for a luxury resort — a five-star ecotourism site, as his wife, Ivanka Trump, laid out in a podcast episode called "Ivanka Trump on Building the Authentic Life."

"For me," said Trump, "this is, it feels more like a challenge than anything else, the culmination of all of my experience in real estate, all of my travel, a lot of reflection on how I want to live."

In the podcast, Trump described both the Zvernec beachfront property as well as Sazan — an uninhabited island across from it — as part of a development project belonging to her and Kushner.

Local tour operator Sherif Durmishaj has made a living taking tourists to Sazan by boat, guiding hikes past foxholes and signs along the trail that warn of active land mines scattered throughout the island's forests. For years, this island was a fortified military outpost.

Durmishaj says he's seen the ongoing protests against the Kushner project, but he takes a different view of it.

"I work in tourism, and I'm from here," he says, "and if you've seen how local developers, along with the mafia, have built this region, it's just a massacre. They've destroyed so much of what is a beautiful coastline, and I support the Kushner project because it's going to be ecologically sustainable and it will set a good benchmark for future projects."

Sherif Durmishaj, who gives tours, navigates his boat to Sazan Island off the coast of Albania, which Ivanka Trump has said she and Kushner will someday develop. Durmishaj says he's in favor of Kushner and Trump's proposed resort because he thinks it will set a benchmark for future development along the coast.

Rob Schmitz/NPR

hide caption

Rob Schmitz/NPR

"We are a small country," Durmishaj says, "and Kushner and Trump are very big names."

blocks.alt: Sunset over the southern Albanian coast along the Adriatic Sea. Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump say they plan to build a luxury resort along the coast, a development that has been met with daily protests in the capital, Tirana.

blocks.text:
The sun sets over coastal mountains near the city of Vlore, the region where Jared Kushner plans to build a five-star luxury resort. The land that Kushner bought for this project, though, is claimed by several local Albanians and its ownership is being investigated by state prosecutors.

Rob Schmitz/NPR

hide caption
Rob Schmitz/NPR

ZVERNEC, Albania — In the summer of 2021, Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump boarded a yacht owned by Nat Rothschild, an heir to the European banking family. On the way from Montenegro to Greece, the yacht anchored off the coast of Albania.
And, as Kushner told an investment conference last year, that's when Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama arrived at the boat to tell them about his plan for the country.

"I was very impressed by what he wanted to do with the country," said Kushner. "I really didn't know anything about the country and I didn't understand the history, and the darkness of the history with the communism and terrible leadership led to it being fully undeveloped as a nation."

A year later, Kushner was looking for development opportunities in the Balkans. He returned to the Albanian coast — to the city of Vlore, which was finishing the construction of an airport atop a wetland near an undeveloped coastline. "And obviously, a country's going to build an airport by the coast in a place they think is most beautiful," Kushner told the conference, "so we went there and we were looking for opportunities, and we found some incredible opportunities."

Kushner found those opportunities at Hidrovor Beach, an expanse of caramel-colored sand along the southern Albanian coast, with the gentle waves of the Adriatic lapping its perimeter and a view of an uninhabited island. A company working for Kushner purchased this land and 300 acres surrounding it for more than $130 million in April. But several people here tell NPR this is not Kushner's land.
They say it's theirs.

The land is now slated to be developed for a luxury hotel owned by Jared Kushner and Ivanka Trump. In the background is Sazan Island, a publicly owned island that Trump and Kushner also say they will develop.

Land grabs and falsified documents

"This land here belonged to my family for centuries," says Gentian Mocka, who claims his family has owned this strip of beach and wetland since the time of the Ottoman Empire. He provided NPR land titles that appear to prove this.
After World War II, Albania's Communist government seized it — along with all private land.

When communism fell in 1991, families like Mocka's embarked on a years-long process to get their land back. "But then our problems started with the guys that were much more powerful than we were — had a lot of political support, were very rich and very well connected with the politics of that time," says Mocka.

In 2005, Mocka learned that someone else was laying claim to his family's land — a fellow Albanian named Artur Shehu. It was a familiar name for those who lived here in the 1990s, when the regional capital of Vlore was outside the control of the country's government. It was instead run by mafia-style gangs. At the time, Shehu was well-known to police in Vlore for his alleged involvement in a crime syndicate that, according to Albanian prosecutors, smuggled drugs and migrants into Europe. He fled Albania in 1999, after what police say was a shootout with a rival gang.

He ended up in the United States, where he received asylum in 2001 and, later, became a U.S. citizen. The 60-year-old Shehu now lives in a villa in Miami Beach. But he's continued to manage a growing real estate portfolio back in Albania through an associate in Vlore named Pellumb Petritaj.

The pair has claimed plots of land — including Mocka's family plot — up and down the southern Albanian coast, and prosecutors have taken notice. In 2018, Petritaj served three years in prison for forging land titles on behalf of Shehu. And on Nov. 18, Petritaj was sentenced to another seven years in prison for falsifying documents to $17 million worth of oceanfront property in the city of Vlore on behalf of Shehu. The court ordered the land — which does not include Mocka's family plot — confiscated from Shehu last week. The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.
Albanian prosecutors say land linked to Kushner may have been "illegally acquired"
The pair has also claimed oceanfront farmland in the village of Zvernec, adjacent to Mocka's land.

The quiet village has only a couple hundred residents. Most of them, like Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota, are past the age of 70. On a recent warm and sunny afternoon, the two are resting on benches in the courtyard of the village church after a day of harvesting olives. They nod their heads when asked about Artur Shehu.
"He is from the village of Kanina, far from here and up in the mountains," says Konomi, motioning inland, "but his family has never lived here. He's involved in shady dealings."

Then Kota speaks up. "There wasn't a single soul of that family living here, going back to the Ottoman times," she says. "But we've heard stories about him, and we're very scared of him."

Twenty years ago, Kota, Konomi and dozens of others in this village learned that Artur Shehu had somehow acquired their farmland. They filed suit in Albanian court to reclaim their land, a fight that escalated this past April when Shehu sold the 300-acre parcel that includes what they say is their farmland to a company developing a luxury resort project for Kushner.
That transaction, however, is under review.
In court documents obtained by NPR, Albanian prosecutors argue that the land involved in Kushner's development is "suspected of having been illegally acquired through forgery."

A spokesman for Kushner did not respond to NPR's request for comment by the time this article was published. Kushner had previously issued a statement on his website saying his partnership purchased the land from a private party in a private transaction. "Title was reviewed by counsel and verified," the statement says.
Shehu did not respond to NPR's request for comment. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. However, in Tirana, a former lawyer for Shehu was willing to talk.
Oceanfront properties are now claimed by several parties

"The people that Artur [Shehu] has authorized by power of attorney to deal with his family's properties committed a forgery in which they removed the property from the brother of Artur's grandfather and passed it to Artur's grandfather," says Kujtim Cakrani. "That is the whole story of the property."

Cakrani says Shehu's associates forged an inheritance certificate that made it appear that Shehu's grandfather had owned the land, which was then passed to Artur Shehu himself. And then last April, Shehu sold that land to Moutaz and Ramez Al-Khayyat, Syrian-born Qatari billionaire brothers who are financial partners of Jared Kushner.

Cakrani says that when he discovered that Artur Shehu was involved in this alleged forgery, he dropped him as his client. "I could no longer continue representing him because of the seriousness of the matter," he says. "It is impossible for me, with these documents that he has, to defend him."

And this is why, Cakrani says, Albanian state prosecutors have put Shehu under investigation and froze his bank accounts. Cakrani says he is now representing a group of 30 relatives of Shehu who he claims to be the rightful owners of this land.

Gentian Mocka, as well as Minella Konomi and Natasha Kota in Zvernec, tell NPR that nobody by the name of Shehu — neither Artur nor his relatives — has any legal claim to what they say is their land, oceanfront property that has now been claimed by several parties, including the son-in-law of the president of the United States.
Wealthy speculators have exploited land in Albania since the fall of communism
Albanian real estate law expert Roden Hoxha says he has seen this kind of land battle many times before. "But now that Kushner is in it," he says, "everybody is freaking out."

He says land ownership in Albania is complicated by decades under a Stalinist regime that stole all the land from private owners and collectivized it. When communism fell in 1991, he says Albania became a land grab free-for-all.
"It was basically chaos," he says. "People started claiming land wherever they threw a stone. It was basically the Albanian version of the U.S.' claiming of the West."

Hoxha describes wealthy speculators keen to exploit the chaos of the moment: locals whose families have farmed the land for generations and well-connected operators like Shehu, who aggressively try to claim that land. "And then on the international level," says Hoxha, most recently, "it exploded because it was Kushner and Trump and Arab money behind it."

And so, Hoxha says, what at first appeared to be yet another Albanian land dispute now has ties all the way to the White House. In the end, an Albanian court will likely decide who the rightful owner of this property is. But for now, it has sparked unprecedented public outrage in Albania. Protesters have taken to the streets of the capital, Tirana, every day since May 31, calling on Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. But Rama has only vowed to crack down harder on what have become increasingly violent demonstrations against his entire government.
Rama has also vowed that Kushner's resort project will go ahead as planned, but an ongoing investigation by Albania's state prosecutor into forged land titles could halt the project.

When contacted by NPR, Elona Sinaj, Rama's spokesperson, sent a statement saying, "If the seller does not have legitimate ownership of the property, the money will remain within the Republic of Albania, and certainly it will be used for anyone who proves that his claim over the property is grounded."
Sinaj went on to say that the ambition for Rama's government is "to create a new benchmark for sustainable Mediterranean development."
Some Albanians see advantages to having a Kushner-linked resort

That goal aligns with Kushner's vision for a luxury resort — a five-star ecotourism site, as his wife, Ivanka Trump, laid out in a podcast episode called "Ivanka Trump on Building the Authentic Life."

"For me," said Trump, "this is, it feels more like a challenge than anything else, the culmination of all of my experience in real estate, all of my travel, a lot of reflection on how I want to live."
In the podcast, Trump described both the Zvernec beachfront property as well as Sazan — an uninhabited island across from it — as part of a development project belonging to her and Kushner.

Local tour operator Sherif Durmishaj has made a living taking tourists to Sazan by boat, guiding hikes past foxholes and signs along the trail that warn of active land mines scattered throughout the island's forests. For years, this island was a fortified military outpost.
Durmishaj says he's seen the ongoing protests against the Kushner project, but he takes a different view of it.

"I work in tourism, and I'm from here," he says, "and if you've seen how local developers, along with the mafia, have built this region, it's just a massacre. They've destroyed so much of what is a beautiful coastline, and I support the Kushner project because it's going to be ecologically sustainable and it will set a good benchmark for future projects."

items.title: Is North Korea holding back on sending Russia more troops?
items.summary: A North Korean troop buildup Ukraine warned about months ago has yet to materialize, even as strategic cooperation continues. Analysts say Pyongyang is balancing its ties with Moscow and Beijing.

Over the summer, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that he expected between 30,000 and 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to Russia as part of Pyongyang's ongoing support of Moscow's war effort.

However, it now appears that troop buildup has yet to materialize, and it is unclear whether North Korea will continue sending large numbers of troops to Russia.

Writing on Telegram on November 9, Andrii Kovalenko, who resigned in September as head of Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, said an August intelligence assessment indicated that the Kremlin had requested more than 30,000 additional North Korean troops for an autumn offensive.

He said a summit between North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin was expected in September, but did not happen. Kviy has claimed that North Korea previously sent thousands of troops to Russia's Kursk region in 2024, where Moscow was fighting to repel a Ukrainian incursion.

Kovalenko believes Pyongyang turned down Moscow's request because taking part in offensive operations in Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine's Donetsk region may still be a red line for North Korea.

However, Kovalenko added that Russia still relies on North Korean material support, particularly ammunition, while assessing that another major deployment of North Korean combat troops was unlikely this winter.

No need for North Korean reinforcements?

Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, told DW that the lull in fighting and the onset of winter give Pyongyang little immediate reason to send reinforcements.

North Korea expands role in Russia's war with Ukraine

He added that a visit this week to Moscow by Jo Yong-won, a senior North Korean official and close aide to Kim, could shed light on any future plans.

Han said it remained to be seen whether the visit was intended to deepen political ties between the ruling parties, building on their military cooperation, or to lay the groundwork for a visit by Kim himself.

Ahn Chan-il, a former North Korean soldier who defected to South Korea in 1979 and now heads the World Institute for North Korea Studies in Seoul, said Moscow also had reasons to limit the deployment.

He told DW that he expects Russia to weigh its battlefield needs against the costs of bringing in more North Korean troops. Unless the war expands, he said, Moscow is unlikely to request a larger contingent.

North Korean weapons keep flowing

Ukrainian official Kovalenko said North Korea still had a missile unit in Russia's Voronezh region and around 8,500 support personnel in rear areas, including drone operators, engineers and sappers.

He added that Pyongyang was ramping up ammunition production and showcasing new drones and missiles.

In a post on X on November 17, Zelenskyy said that Russia was receiving dozens of North Korean ballistic missiles each month.

He warned that their use in Ukraine was helping Pyongyang refine its weapons and creating security risks for countries around the Korean Peninsula. Battle-testing weaponry is one of North Korea's primary advantages from military cooperation with Russia

Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs

Balancing Russia and China ties

Kovalenko said Pyongyang appeared to have adopted what he called a "containment strategy," limiting its military commitment to Russia's war while maintaining ties with both Moscow and Beijing.

In his assessment, this approach allows Pyongyang to retain the benefits of its alliance with Russia while reducing its exposure to the outcome of the war.

Analyst Ahn said he expects Pyongyang's military cooperation with Moscow to continue because Russian assistance is crucial to North Korea's efforts to develop drone technology and strengthen its navy.

Nevertheless, the extent of this cooperation may be more limited in the future, and Pyongyang is also able to turn to China as a hedge.

Ahn said that if Russia limits the deployment of North Korean troops, Pyongyang's foreign currency earnings from those deployments would have less room to grow, giving it another reason to seek more support from Beijing

Jeong Joon Hee, a former South Korean Unification Ministry spokesperson, told DW that recent moves towards building better ties with Beijing may also reflect Pyongyang's dissatisfaction with what Moscow has offered in return for North Korea's help.

By strengthening its relationship with China while keeping ties with Russia steady, he said, Pyongyang could also be trying to persuade Moscow to give it more.

Kim Hyung Suk, a former South Korean vice minister of unification, told DW that North Korea needs China's economic, political and diplomatic backing alongside the support it receives from Russia. He expects Pyongyang to keep pursuing China's support regardless of how it manages its role in the war.
